ta-l1d12q1-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 12. Having shown that the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son, Lombard asks whether there is any order between Father and Son in this procession. He excludes an order of time (with a heretic's objection and Augustine's answer to such 'laborious rather than fruitful' questions) and an order of dignity or power, since the Spirit does not proceed more fully from the Father than from the Son. He affirms an order of nature, shown by four signs of the Father's authority in spiration: the Spirit proceeds from the Father 'principally', 'properly', and 'through the Son', and sometimes only the Father is named in the procession. Three articles are announced: whether the Son's generation precedes the Spirit's procession, whether the Spirit proceeds earlier or more fully from the Father, and whether he proceeds from the Father through the Son as a medium.
claims: There is no order of time or dignity between Father and Son in spiration, only an order of nature.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3538.summary: First argument that generation precedes procession. The principle of a procession is naturally prior to it, and the principle of the Spirit's procession is the Son, the terminus of generation.
claims: A principle of procession is naturally prior to the procession.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3541.summary: Second argument. In creatures the action of nature precedes the action of will, which is founded on it. The Son is from the Father by way of nature and the Spirit from both by way of will, so generation is prior.
claims: Natural action precedes voluntary action.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3544.summary: Third argument. In the image in the soul, the procession of knowledge from the mind precedes the procession of love, and these represent the generation of the Son and the procession of the Spirit.
claims: In the image, knowledge precedes love.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3548.summary: Sed contra from Lombard's text: the Spirit does not proceed 'with the Son already born', which would have to be the case if birth preceded procession.
claims: The Spirit does not proceed after the Son is born.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3551.summary: Second sed contra. The Spirit stands to the Son in the order of origin as the Son to the Father, and the Father is in no way prior to the Son (Dist. 9), so neither is the Son prior to the Spirit, nor generation to procession.
claims: As the Father is not prior to the Son, the Son is not prior to the Spirit.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3554.summary: Thomas's determination. According to Augustine there is no order in God except an order of nature, by which one is from another, not one before another. So nothing in God can be called prior. In God one can consider only what is absolute, which is one and indivisible and has no priority, or what is relative, and relatives are simultaneous in time, understanding, and nature. So generation is not prior to procession in any way that can be referred to God, but only in our mode of understanding, which grasps them through creaturely likenesses that fail to represent them.
claims: In God there is only an order of nature, by which one is from another, without priority.
Generation precedes procession only in our mode of understanding.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3557.summary: Reply to the first argument. A principle, as related, is in no way prior to what it originates, though what is a principle is naturally prior. If the one who is a principle is someone, a distinct person, by that very relation, all priority is removed. The Son is a distinct person by his relation, so he is in no way prior to the Spirit. Still, by the order of nature the Spirit is from the Son. Common spiration is not the Son's personal property, yet it is the Son's very person, as divine goodness is God himself, and the first procession corresponding to it is the Spirit's personal property.
claims: The Son, constituted by his relation, is not prior to the Spirit, though the Spirit is from him by order of nature.
Common spiration is not the Son's personal property but is identical with his person.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3560.summary: Reply to the second and third arguments. They fail because creaturely likenesses do not perfectly represent what is in God. No creature has from the same source both being relative and being self-subsistent.
claims: Creaturely analogies of nature and will, knowledge and love, fail to represent divine order.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3572.summary: First argument that the Spirit proceeds more from the Father than from the Son. Every primary cause influences its effect more than a secondary cause (the Philosopher, Liber de causis), and the Son is like a secondary cause, while the Father is the first principle not from a principle.
claims: A primary cause influences more than a secondary one.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3575.summary: Second argument from the Philosopher: that on account of which each thing is such is more such. The Son has from the Father his being the principle of the Spirit, so the Father is more a principle.
claims: Propter quod unumquodque tale, et illud magis.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3581.summary: Third argument. What is principle of something principally and properly is more its principle. According to Lombard's text the Spirit proceeds from the Father principally and properly, which is not said of the Son.
claims: The Spirit proceeds principaliter et proprie from the Father.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3585.summary: Fourth argument. The Spirit has nothing that he does not have from the Father, but he has something he does not have from the Son, namely that he proceeds from the Father.
claims: The Spirit has from the Father something he does not have from the Son.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3591.summary: Second sed contra. Where there is supreme equality there can be no 'more' or 'more fully', and there is supreme equality between Father and Son.
claims: Supreme equality excludes degrees.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3594.summary: Thomas's determination. The Spirit proceeds neither earlier, nor more fully, nor more from the Father than from the Son. The whole reason is that Father and Son are one principle of the Spirit, and where there is unity there can be no distinction of fullness.
claims: Father and Son are one principle of the Spirit, so he proceeds equally from both.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3597.summary: Reply to the first argument. Although the Father is called principle of Son and Spirit, he cannot properly be called their cause, since a cause always implies diversity of essence, whereas a principle from which something flows can be consubstantial with it, as a point is the principle of a line, the heart of an animal, the foundation of a house. A cause also implies dependence, while a principle implies only origin, that from which something begins. Nor can the Father be called 'first', since there is no prior and posterior in God. So the authority does not apply. Even setting this aside, Father and Son relate to the Spirit not as two principles but as one, so there is no gradation between them in spirating.
claims: The Father is principle, not cause, of Son and Spirit, since cause implies diversity of essence and dependence.
Father and Son are one principle of the Spirit, with no gradation.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3600.summary: Reply to the second argument. The Philosopher's dictum holds when what belongs to one because of another differs in the two, especially when one is cause of the other in an essential causal order, as heat is more in fire than in a mixed body, which has it because of fire (Avicenna). The Son has from the Father his spirating, but the spirative power is not diverse in them: the Father communicates the same power to the Son, so they spirate equally. Even if it were the same only in species, the argument would fail, as in univocal generation Socrates' father does not influence Socrates' son more than Socrates does.
claims: The Father communicates numerically the same spirative power to the Son, so they spirate equally.
'Propter quod' applies only when the quality differs in the two.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3604.summary: Reply to the third argument. The Spirit is said to be 'principally' from the Father because the authority of spiration is in the Father, from whom the Son has spirative power, not because of any order or degree of priority. For the same reason he is said to proceed 'properly' from the Father, especially since among the Greeks the preposition 'from' marks relation to the first origin: they say a lake is from the spring, not from the stream, which is why they do not grant that the Spirit is from the Son. Yet the Spirit also proceeds properly from the Son, who is one principle with the Father, unlike stream and spring, which are not one principle of the lake.
claims: 'Principaliter' and 'proprie' signify the Father's authority of origin, not a degree of priority.
Greek usage of 'from' for first origin explains their reluctance about the filioque.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3607.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The Spirit does not proceed from the Father otherwise or by another procession than from the Son, so the whole procession is from the Son as it is wholly from the Father, and nothing in the Spirit is not from the Son. The procession is not from the Son in every respect, but this does not lessen its fullness. It is incidental to the procession that, in the respect in which it is from the Son, it is from the Father, not because the Spirit is from the Son but because the Son is from the Father.
claims: The whole procession of the Spirit is from the Son as it is wholly from the Father.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3619.summary: First argument that the Spirit proceeds from the Father mediately through the Son. That through which something proceeds is a medium, and the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son.
claims: What one proceeds through is a medium.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3622.summary: Second argument. A third comes from a first only through a middle, and the Spirit is the third person, so he proceeds from the Father, the principle without principle, only through the Son.
claims: A third proceeds from a first only through a middle.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3625.summary: Third argument. In the created image, love proceeds from the mind only through knowledge.
claims: In the image, love proceeds from mind through knowledge.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3629.summary: Contrary argument, that the Spirit proceeds more immediately from the Father than from the Son. An immediate principle is more principal than a mediate one, as first propositions are called immediate, and the Spirit proceeds principally from the Father.
claims: An immediate principle is more principal.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3632.summary: Thomas's determination. Every medium is in some way distinct from what it mediates. Father and Son are two spirators who are one in spirative power, so spiration can be considered with respect to the spirators or to the principle by whose power spiration occurs. As to the principle, the spirative power, Father and Son are not distinguished, so spiration is not from the Father through the Son as medium. As to the spirators, who are distinct and furnish the supposit of spiration, there is mediation according to the order of nature, since the Son is from the Father and the Spirit from both together. So Richard of St Victor says that generation is from the Father immediately, while the Spirit's procession is in a way mediate and in a way immediate. It is immediate as to the spirative power, which is one in Father and Son, and as to the Father's supposit, which immediately spirates together with the Son. It is mediate insofar as the Son, who spirates, is from the Father.
claims: As to spirative power the Spirit proceeds immediately from the Father; as to the spirating persons he proceeds mediately, through the Son who is from the Father.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3635.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'From the Father through the Son' designates the Father's authority with respect to the Son, since the Son has from the Father his spirating. This implies mediation only on the side of the supposits, which are distinguished by one being from the other, by reason of which one has authority with respect to the other.
claims: 'Per filium' signifies the Father's authority, and mediation only of supposits.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3638.summary: Reply to the second argument. In one way the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, but this does not exclude his also proceeding immediately from the Father.
claims: Mediate procession does not exclude immediate procession.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3641.summary: Reply to the third argument. The image in the soul represents the Trinity deficiently: knowledge is wholly distinct from the mind, so love proceeds from the mind simply through knowledge. In God the Son is not distinguished from the Father in everything, so in some respect there is no mediation.
claims: Because the Son is not distinguished from the Father in everything, his mediation is only partial.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3644.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. When several ordered agent causes act, one can consider the agent exercising the action or its power, the principle of the action. As to the agent, the later it is, the more proximate and immediate to the action and its product. As to the power, the more primary the cause, the more immediate it is, since a secondary agent acts only as moved by the first and as the first's power is in it, so the power of the last agent always resolves into that of the first. For example, a plant generates a plant by the sun's power, and the sun moves to generation by the power of its mover. So God, as first agent, is by his power more immediate to every operation of nature than any natural agent, and first propositions are called immediate because no prior cause joins predicate to subject. The preposition 'through' (per), denoting a middle cause, can mark authority in the direct case ('the king acts through his bailiff', mediation of agents) or the oblique ('the provost acts through the king', mediation of power). In Father and Son the principle of operation, divine power, is the same; they differ only as agents. Since the Father has authority, the Father is said to act through the Son and never the Son through the Father. In a way the Son is a medium in the Father's operation, but the Father is never a medium in the Son's.
claims: Among ordered causes, the last agent is most immediate as agent, the first is most immediate as power.
God, as first agent, is more immediate in power to every natural operation than any natural agent.
The Father acts through the Son, never the Son through the Father, because the Father has authority.

ta-l1d12q1-d1e3654.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'Either with the Son already born or not yet born' seems to force one alternative, since affirmation and negation differ. Both are ambiguous. If the participle signifies past time and the adverb the moment just before the present, the affirmative is false, implying that generation precedes procession in duration, and the negative is true taken as negating the whole. If the participle signifies the perfection of the birth and the adverb the 'now' of eternity, the affirmative is true, since the Spirit proceeds eternally while the Son's generation is complete, and the negative is false. (2) 'More fully' and 'more' differ: one proceeds more fully from the one from whom one receives more, more from the one who works with greater power. (3) 'Principally from the Father' does not imply 'secondarily from the Son', because 'principally' marks not degree of power but order of origin, since the Son has his spirating from the Father.
claims: 'Jam nato filio' is true if 'jam' means the 'now' of eternity and false if temporal.
'Principaliter' signifies order of origin, not degree of power.

ta-l1d12q1-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 12 maps Lombard's exclusion of an order of time and of dignity between Father and Son in spiration and his affirmation of an order of nature, shown by the Father's authority. It announces three articles accordingly.

ta-l1d12q1-Dd1e3530.summary: Article 1 asks whether the Son's generation precedes the Spirit's procession. Thomas holds, with Augustine, that in God there is only an order of nature, by which one is from another without priority. The essence is indivisible and relatives are simultaneous, so generation precedes procession only in our mode of understanding. The Son, constituted by his relation, is not prior to the Spirit, though the Spirit is from him, and common spiration is identical with the Son's person without being his personal property.
claims: Generation does not precede procession in God, only in our understanding.
In God there is order of nature without priority.

ta-l1d12q1-Dd1e3564.summary: Article 2 asks whether the Spirit proceeds earlier or more fully from the Father. Thomas holds that he proceeds neither earlier, nor more fully, nor more from the Father, since Father and Son are one principle. The Father is properly principle, not cause, of the other persons, and he is not 'first'. He communicates numerically the same spirative power to the Son. 'Principally' and 'properly' signify the Father's authority of origin, and the whole procession is from the Son as it is wholly from the Father.
claims: The Spirit proceeds equally from Father and Son, who are one principle.
The Father is principle, not cause, of the Son and Spirit.

ta-l1d12q1-Dd1e3611.summary: Article 3 asks whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son as medium. Distinguishing spirators from the spirative power, Thomas holds with Richard of St Victor that the procession is immediate as to the one power and as to the Father's supposit, and mediate insofar as the spirating Son is from the Father. A general analysis of ordered causes shows that the last agent is most immediate as agent and the first most immediate as power, so God is more immediate in power to every natural operation than any creature. 'Per' can mark mediation of agents or of power, so the Father acts through the Son, never the Son through the Father.
claims: The Spirit proceeds from the Father both immediately (in power) and mediately (through the Son as spirating person).
In ordered causes, the first is most immediate in power and the last in agency.

ta-l1d12q1-Dd1e3649.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 12 resolves the dilemma 'with the Son already born or not' by distinguishing temporal and eternal senses of 'jam'. It distinguishes 'more fully' from 'more', and it reads 'principally' as order of origin rather than degree of power.
claims: 'Principaliter' signifies order of origin, not degree.

ta-l1d12q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 12 asks about order between Father and Son in the Spirit's procession. Article 1 holds that in God there is only an order of nature, origin without priority, so the Son's generation precedes the Spirit's procession only in our understanding. Article 2 holds that the Spirit proceeds equally from Father and Son, who are one principle with numerically the same spirative power. The Father's being 'principal' and 'proper' principle expresses his authority of origin, not a degree, and the Father is principle, not cause, of the other persons. Article 3 holds that the procession is both immediate, in the one power, and mediate, through the Son as a spirating person who is from the Father. It grounds this in a general theory of ordered causes, on which God is most immediate in power to every operation. The Expositio resolves related dilemmas.
claims: In God there is order of nature without priority; generation does not precede procession.
The Spirit proceeds equally from Father and Son as one principle; the Father's primacy is one of authority, not degree.
The procession is immediate in power and mediate through the Son as person.
